::: {.oneline}
A field is a physical system carrying a degree of freedom at every point of
space, and the objects we call particles are its vibrations, counted out in
fixed units.
:::

## Short answer

Consider a mattress, that is, a grid of springs, each able to move and each
pulling on its neighbours. If we push it somewhere, the disturbance travels. A
field is this picture taken to the limit: not a grid, but a value attached to
every point of space, with neighbouring points coupled so that disturbances
propagate at finite speed.

Since the couplings are local, an arbitrary disturbance is complicated, but we
can always rewrite it as a sum of simple standing patterns, each oscillating at
its own steady rate and none of them disturbing the others. These patterns are
the natural language of the field, and each of them behaves exactly like a
single pendulum.

Quantum mechanics then applies to each pattern separately, and a pendulum in
quantum mechanics has energies climbing in equal steps. Counting the steps in a
pattern is therefore counting particles. This is why a field theory produces
particles at all: not as an additional assumption, but as the only way in which
a quantum oscillator is allowed to store energy.

## Why it works this way

Fields are the way in which physics preserves causality. If two distant objects
interact, either the influence jumps across instantaneously (which relativity
forbids) or something carries it, point by point, at finite speed. A field is
that something, and everything else, including the existence of particles,
follows from insisting on locality and then quantizing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: normal modes

For a free field $\phi$ obeying a linear wave equation, expanding in normal
modes diagonalizes the energy,

$$
H = \sum_{\mathbf k} \left( \frac{|p_{\mathbf k}|^2}{2}
+ \frac{\omega_{\mathbf k}^2 |q_{\mathbf k}|^2}{2} \right),
$$ {#eq-normal-modes}

which is a set of independent harmonic oscillators labelled by $\mathbf k$.
Canonical quantization of each one gives a ladder of states separated by
$\hbar\omega_{\mathbf k}$. Interactions spoil the exact decoupling, and are what
make the problem both hard and interesting.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"A field is just a mathematical device for computing forces."** It carries
  energy and momentum, and both are measurable. The vacuum energy of the
  electromagnetic field between two plates produces a measurable force.
- **"Particles are fundamental, and fields describe how many there are."** The
  logic runs in the opposite direction, since the field is the object and
  particle number is a label on its state.
